spark.summary: Modern API security pairs OAuth 2.0 (for delegated user/client authorization), signed JWTs (for stateless, verifiable claims), and Mutual TLS (mTLS) (for cryptographic workload and high-assurance client identity).
spark.keyTakeaway: Use mTLS to prove *who the calling machine is* at the transport layer, and short-lived OAuth2/JWT tokens to prove *what the user or client is authorized to do* at the application layer.

concept.whyItMatters: Bearer tokens alone are vulnerable to theft and replay—anyone holding a leaked JWT can call an API until it expires. Combining OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code + PKCE, asymmetric RS256/EdDSA JWTs (5–15 min TTL), and mTLS (RFC 8705 certificate-bound tokens) ensures stolen tokens are useless without the client's private key and eliminates shared static API secrets.
whenToUse: Exposing user-facing APIs to SPAs, mobile apps, or third-party integrations requiring fine-grained OAuth2 scopes and consent.
Securing B2B financial/healthcare APIs (e.g., Open Banking, FAPI 2.0) where tokens must be cryptographically bound to the caller's X.509 client certificate via mTLS.
Authenticating zero-trust microservice-to-microservice calls using workload identities (SPIFFE/SPIRE or Istio mTLS) plus propagated user JWTs.
whenNotToUse: Simple internal scripts or single-tenant webhooks where HMAC-SHA256 request signing is simpler than standing up an OAuth2 Authorization Server.
Static public read-only APIs (e.g., weather feeds or public docs) where API keys for basic quota tracking suffice.
Environments where you need instant, sub-second global session revocation across all services without maintaining a token introspection or revocation cache.
keyPoints: OAuth 2.0 is authorization, not authentication: use OpenID Connect (OIDC) `id_token` for user identity and OAuth2 `access_token` for API permissions (`scope`, `aud`).
Always use Authorization Code + PKCE (RFC 7636) for public clients (SPAs, mobile); the Implicit (`response_type=token`) and Resource Owner Password Credentials flows are deprecated in OAuth 2.1.
Stateless JWT validation checks `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, and the cryptographic signature against the Identity Provider's JWKS endpoint—no DB lookup per request.
mTLS (TLS 1.3) requires both server and client to present X.509 certificates during the handshake, authenticating the caller's machine identity before HTTP bytes are parsed.
Sender-constrained tokens (RFC 8705 `cnf.x5t#S256`) embed the SHA-256 thumbprint of the client's mTLS certificate inside the JWT, stopping bearer-token replay dead.

examples.title: FAPI-Compliant Payment API with mTLS-Bound JWTs
examples.scenario: A fintech partner calls `POST /transfers` using an OAuth2 access token obtained via `client_credentials` with an mTLS client certificate.
examples.outcome: The gateway verifies the TLS client cert thumbprint matches the JWT's `cnf.x5t#S256` claim; a token exfiltrated to another host fails with `401 Unauthorized` even before expiration.

examples.title: Zero-Trust Service Mesh with Workload mTLS + End-User JWT
examples.scenario: An API gateway forwards a customer's `GET /orders` request through an internal aggregator to the Orders microservice.
examples.outcome: Istio enforces SPIFFE mTLS between pods (`spiffe://cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/gateway`) while the Orders service checks the end-user JWT `sub` and `scope` for row-level authorization.

tradeOffs.factor: Stateless JWT vs. Opaque Token + Introspection
tradeOffs.pro: JWTs validate locally in <100 µs via cached JWKS with zero network hop to the auth server.
tradeOffs.con: Revoking a compromised JWT before its `exp` (e.g., 15 min) requires a distributed denylist or short TTLs.

tradeOffs.pro: Private keys never traverse the wire, preventing credential stuffing and secret leaks in logs.
tradeOffs.con: Requires automated PKI lifecycle management (cert-manager, SPIRE, or ACME) to avoid outages from expired certs.

tradeOffs.factor: Coarse Scopes vs. Fine-Grained Claims in JWT
tradeOffs.pro: Embedding all permissions in the token avoids downstream authorization DB queries.
tradeOffs.con: Bloats HTTP `Authorization` headers beyond 4–8 KB, triggering `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`.

failureModes.name: Expired mTLS Intermediate or Leaf Certificate
failureModes.description: A missed certificate rotation breaks the TLS handshake across all B2B or service-to-service callers simultaneously, causing 100% outage.
failureModes.mitigation: Automate short-lived certs (24h–30d) via SPIRE or cert-manager, support dual-root CA overlap during rotation, and alert at 30% remaining TTL.

failureModes.name: Missing `aud` or `alg` Validation in JWT Verifier
failureModes.description: Accepting `alg: none`, symmetric HS256 with an RSA public key, or omitting `aud` lets an attacker forge tokens or replay tokens minted for another API.
failureModes.mitigation: Pin allowed asymmetric algorithms (`RS256`, `ES256`, `EdDSA`) explicitly in code and strictly assert `iss` and `aud` on every route.

failureModes.name: JWKS Rotation Outage
failureModes.description: IdP rotates its signing key (`kid`), but gateways with stale 24-hour JWKS caches reject all newly minted tokens with `401`.
failureModes.mitigation: Trigger an asynchronous, rate-limited JWKS refresh on unknown `kid` cache misses (e.g., max 1 refresh per 10s).

failureModes.name: Token Leakage in Logs or URLs
failureModes.description: Passing JWTs in query strings (`?access_token=...`) or logging full request headers exposes live credentials in proxy access logs and browser history.
failureModes.mitigation: Accept tokens strictly in `Authorization: Bearer` headers and redact `Authorization` and `Cookie` fields in all structured loggers.

commonMistakes: Using `alg: HS256` with a shared secret across multiple untrusted microservices instead of asymmetric `RS256`/`EdDSA` keys.
Setting JWT lifetimes to 24+ hours without refresh token rotation, creating a huge window of exposure if a token is stolen.
Storing OAuth2 access tokens in browser `localStorage` instead of using the BFF pattern with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax` cookies.
Terminating mTLS at an edge load balancer and forwarding plain HTTP internally without passing a verified `X-Client-Cert` hash or re-originating mTLS.
Putting PII or sensitive roles inside unencrypted JWT payloads (base64url is encoding, not encryption—use JWE if payload confidentiality is needed).

sections.content:
## The idea

API security breaks down into two orthogonal questions: **Who is the calling software/machine?** and **What is the user or client allowed to do?** Mutual TLS (mTLS) answers the first at the transport layer using X.509 certificates during the TLS 1.3 handshake. OAuth 2.0 and signed JWTs answer the second at the application layer using scoped, short-lived tokens. Binding the two together (RFC 8705) ties an application token to a cryptographic transport identity so neither a stolen token nor an unauthorized host can succeed alone.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a high-assurance B2B call from Partner Service to `POST https://api.bank.io/v1/wires`:

1. **Token Acquisition (mTLS + OAuth2)**: Partner Service opens a TLS 1.3 connection to `auth.bank.io/oauth/token` presenting its X.509 leaf certificate. Using `grant_type=client_credentials`, it requests `scope=wires:write`.
2. **Sender-Constrained Minting**: Keycloak/Auth0 verifies the cert against the trusted CA, computes its SHA-256 thumbprint (`x5t#S256`), embeds it in the JWT `cnf` claim with a 5-minute `exp`, and signs it with `ES256`.
3. **API Call over mTLS**: Partner Service dials `api.bank.io` over mTLS and sends `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`.
4. **Dual-Layer Verification**: The API Gateway completes the mTLS handshake, fetches the public key matching the JWT `kid` from cached JWKS, validates `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, and confirms the live client cert's `x5t#S256` matches `jwt.cnf.x5t#S256` before forwarding the request over internal mesh mTLS.

sections.content:
## OAuth 2.1 flows and token anatomy

A JWT consists of three base64url-encoded parts (`header.payload.signature`). The header declares `alg` (prefer `EdDSA` or `ES256` over `HS256`) and `kid` for key rotation. The payload carries standard claims: `iss` (issuer), `sub` (subject), `aud` (target API URI), `exp` (expiration, 5–15 min), `scope` (space-delimited permissions), and optionally `cnf` for proof-of-possession.

For user-facing web and mobile apps, **Authorization Code + PKCE** is mandatory: the client generates a random `code_verifier`, sends its SHA-256 `code_challenge` to `/authorize`, and proves possession of the verifier at `/oauth/token`. This prevents authorization code interception attacks even without a client secret.

## Security mechanism comparison

| Mechanism | Layer | Proves Identity Of | Replay Resistance | Latency / Overhead |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **API Key** | L7 Header | Static project/app | None if leaked | Near-zero (hash lookup) |
| **Bearer JWT (OAuth2)** | L7 Header | User + App + Scopes | Low until `exp` (keep <=15m) | <100 µs local signature check |
| **Opaque Token + Introspect** | L7 Header | User + App (revocable) | Instant revocation possible | 2–10 ms IdP network call |
| **mTLS (X.509)** | L4/L5 TLS | Workload / Machine | High (private key stays local) | TLS 1.3 handshake (~1 RTT) |
| **mTLS + Bound JWT (RFC 8705)** | L5 + L7 | Machine + User + Scopes | Very high (key-bound token) | TLS handshake + <100 µs check |

## Failure modes

1. **Algorithm Confusion Attack**: A library tricked into reading `alg: HS256` uses the server's public RSA key as an HMAC secret, allowing anyone to forge valid tokens. Fix: hardcode an allowlist of asymmetric algorithms (`["ES256", "RS256"]`) in the verifier.
2. **Cross-Service Token Replay (Confused Deputy)**: Service A accepts a JWT whose `aud` is `service-a`, and an attacker replays that same token against Service B if Service B skips `aud` validation. Fix: enforce strict `aud` matching per service.
3. **PKI Expiry Cliff**: Static 1-year mTLS certificates expire unnoticed on a weekend, dropping 100% of partner traffic. Fix: automate short-lived certs (24h–7d) with SPIRE or cert-manager and alert on cert age.
4. **Clock Skew Rejections**: A 90-second NTP drift between the IdP and an API pod causes valid newly issued tokens to fail `nbf` or `iat` checks. Fix: allow a bounded 30–60s clock skew tolerance and run `chrony`.

## Architecture patterns for modern teams

For browser SPAs, avoid storing OAuth2 tokens in `localStorage` where XSS can exfiltrate them; instead use a **Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)** that holds tokens server-side and issues `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` session cookies. For east-west microservice traffic, delegate workload mTLS to a service mesh (Istio or Cilium with SPIFFE IDs) so developers never manage PEM files in application containers, while keeping application-level RBAC/ABAC tied to the verified JWT claims.

## Practical checklist

- **Enforce OAuth 2.1**: use Authorization Code + PKCE for all user flows and `client_credentials` (with mTLS or `private_key_jwt`) for M2M.
- **Keep access tokens short-lived**: set `exp` to 5–15 minutes and use rotating, single-use refresh tokens.
- **Validate all 5 JWT invariants**: `alg` allowlist, signature via JWKS `kid`, `iss`, `aud`, and `exp`/`nbf`.
- **Bind high-value tokens**: enable RFC 8705 `cnf.x5t#S256` (mTLS) or DPoP for financial, admin, and PII endpoints.
- **Automate cert rotation**: deploy cert-manager or SPIRE with overlapping trust bundles and test rotation in staging monthly.

options.text: HS256 tokens can only be read on Windows servers.

interviewProblems.title: Zero-Trust Financial API Security Mesh
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are designing the security architecture for a banking platform serving 20,000 API requests/sec across 100 internal microservices. How do you implement zero-trust authorization and token revocation?
constraints: Compromised tokens must be revocable within 1 second.

dimensions.name: Stateless JWT Verification & JWKS Cache
dimensions.description: Verifying RS256 JWTs using cached JWKS public keys at API Gateway.

dimensions.name: Redis Revocation Blacklist & mTLS
dimensions.description: Using mTLS for service IPC and Redis bloom filters for token revocation.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Authenticate external calls at Envoy API Gateway via RS256 JWTs verified against cached JWKS. Maintain a Redis revocation blacklist for revoked JTI IDs. Secure inter-service calls using mTLS certificates issued by SPIFFE/SPIRE.
commonPitfalls: Using symmetric secret keys shared across all 100 microservices.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Modern API security pairs OAuth 2.0 (for delegated user/client authorization), signed JWTs (for stateless, verifiable claims), and Mutual TLS (mTLS) (for cryptographic workload and high-assurance client identity).

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: mTLS API Gateway applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Wires Microservice.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Wires Microservice experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Automate short-lived certs (24h–30d) via SPIRE or cert-manager, support dual-root CA overlap during rotation, and alert at 30% remaining TTL.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use mTLS to prove *who the calling machine is* at the transport layer, and short-lived OAuth2/JWT tokens to prove *what the user or client is authorized to do* at the application layer.
Avoid trap: Using `alg: HS256` with a shared secret across multiple untrusted microservices instead of asymmetric `RS256`/`EdDSA` keys.
Avoid trap: Setting JWT lifetimes to 24+ hours without refresh token rotation, creating a huge window of exposure if a token is stolen.
When to reach for it: Exposing user-facing APIs to SPAs, mobile apps, or third-party integrations requiring fine-grained OAuth2 scopes and consent.
When to reach for it: Securing B2B financial/healthcare APIs (e.g., Open Banking, FAPI 2.0) where tokens must be cryptographically bound to the caller's X.509 client certificate via mTLS.

putItTogether.title: Putting Api Security Oauth2 Together
putItTogether.summary: Use mTLS to prove *who the calling machine is* at the transport layer, and short-lived OAuth2/JWT tokens to prove *what the user or client is authorized to do* at the application layer.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Api Security Oauth2 before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: The gateway verifies the TLS client cert thumbprint matches the JWT's `cnf.x5t#S256` claim; a token exfiltrated to another host fails with `401 Unauthorized` even before expiration.
